entities.summary:
Diego de Riaño (born c. 1495, Solórzano, Cantabria – died December 10, 1534, Seville) was a pivotal Spanish architect whose short but prolific career profoundly shaped the early Spanish Renaissance, particularly through his mastery of the Plateresque style. Operating primarily in Seville, his work bridged the late Gothic traditions with the burgeoning Italianate classicism, establishing a distinctly Hispanic architectural idiom. His designs for major ecclesiastical and civic structures, notably the City Hall of Seville and the Sacristy of the Cathedral, exemplify the intricate ornamentation and structural innovation characteristic of the period, making him a central figure in the transition of Spanish architecture into the Early Modern era.

Riaño's architectural education and early career remain somewhat obscure, but by the 1520s, he had established himself in Seville, a burgeoning center of wealth and imperial power. His most significant commission, the Casa Consistorial (City Hall) of Seville, begun around 1527, showcases his mature Plateresque style, blending Gothic structural elements with classical motifs, intricate reliefs, and heraldic symbols. This project, though left incomplete at his death, became a paradigm of municipal architecture, influencing subsequent generations. Concurrently, he was engaged in significant additions to the Seville Cathedral, designing the Sacristy of the Chalices and the Main Sacristy, which display a more classical, albeit still richly decorated, vocabulary.
